Chapter 1 Simple Linear Regression in Stata Our model for a simple bivariate linear regression is the following: \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\] 1.1 Simple Linear Regression Model Using the 2006 General Social Survey, we will look at the association between occupational prestige and hours worked. We will set up our bivariate linear regression model as the following: \[ prestige80_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1 hrs_i + \varepsilon_i \] 1.1.1 Set up your null hypothesis Next, we will set up a null hypothesis: \[ H_{0}: \beta_1 = 0 \] \[ H_{a}: \beta_1 \neq 0 \] Notice for that this will use a two-tailed test instead of a one tailed test. We can set \(\alpha=0.05\), so we will need to look up the critical \(t\) value for \(t_{0.05/2}\) or \(t_{0.025}\). 1.1.2 Descriptive Statistics First, let’s look at the descriptive statistics cd "/Users/Sam/Desktop/Econ 643/AGIS/" use gss2006_chapter8_selected, clear summarize prestg80 hrs1 /Users/Sam/Desktop/Econ 643/AGIS (General Social Surveys, 1972-2006 [Cumulative File], Dataset 0001) Variable | Obs Mean Std. dev. Min Max -------------+--------------------------------------------------------- prestg80 | 4,270 44.16745 13.99946 17 86 hrs1 | 2,739 42.07631 14.23166 1 89 We can see that the dependent variable’s mean is 44.2 with a standard deviation of 14.0 and its range is \([17, 86]\). The independent variable’s mean is 42.1 hours with a standard deviation of 14.2 hours and its range is \([1,89]\) hours per week. Note: There are 4,270 observations with occupational prestige, but only 2,739 have reported hours per week. 1.1.3 Simple Bivariate Linear Regression Next, we will use the regress command to run a linear regression. We use regress \(y\) \(x\) to regress \(y\) onto \(x\). regress prestg80 hrs1 Source | SS df MS Number of obs = 2,715 -------------+---------------------------------- F(1, 2713) = 67.32 Model | 13125.035 1 13125.035 Prob > F = 0.0000 Residual | 528901.224 2,713 194.950691 R-squared = 0.0242 -------------+---------------------------------- Adj R-squared = 0.0239 Total | 542026.259 2,714 199.714908 Root MSE = 13.962 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ prestg80 | Coefficient Std. err. t P>|t| [95% conf. interval] -------------+---------------------------------------------------------------- hrs1 | .1546416 .0188468 8.21 0.000 .117686 .1915972 _cons | 38.14733 .8362129 45.62 0.000 36.50765 39.78701 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Let’s look at these results. We see that: \[ \hat{y} = 38.1 + 0.155x \] 1.1.4 Look up the Critical Values First, let’s find our sample size and get our degrees of freedom. We see that \(n=2,715\) and our \(df=2,714\), so our \(t_{0.025} \approx 1.96\) 1.1.5 Test the Null Hypothesis From our Stata output, we can see that \(t=8.21\) and \(p=0.000\). Using the rejection rule with critical \(t\) values, we see that \(8.21 > 1.96\), so we reject the null hypothesis at the \(5\%\) level. Using the rejection rule with \(p\)-values, we see that \(0.000<0.05\), so we reject the null hypothesis at the \(5\%\) level and conclude that \(\beta_1\) does not equal 0. Furthermore, our \(p\)-value shows that we would reject the null hypothesis at the \(0.1\%\) level, as well. 1.1.6 Goodness of Fit and Sum of Squares We can see our goodness of fit is \(R^2=0.024\) or variation in hours explains \(2.4\%\) of the variation in prestige. Recall that \(R^2=SSE/SST\) or \(R^2=SSR/SST\). We can see this where \(R^2=\frac{13125.035}{542026.259}=0.024\) or \(R^2=1-\frac{528901.224 }{542026.259}=0.024\). 1.1.7 Overall Model One thing we haven’t covered is the \(F\) test statistic. This test statistics shows how the model compares to no model (just an intercept). So, our null hypothesis is that no model is better than our current model. Looking at the \(p\)-value below the \(F\) test statistic, we reject the null hypothesis at the \(0.1\%\) level. 1.2 Predicted \(y\) and Graph Predicted \(y\) We can use the post-estimation command predict to calculate fitted values of \(y\), which we will call \(\hat{y}\) We cannot predict \(\hat{y}\) with the predict command without the regress command. The predict command is a post-estimation command, which means that it must come after a regress command. predict yhat (option xb assumed; fitted values) (1,771 missing values generated) Let’s compare \(y\) and \(\hat{y}\) with a scatter plot. scatter yhat prestg80, jitter(2) title("Prestige and Predicted Prestige") Scatterplot of Prestige and Predicted Prestige We can use a twoway using a lfitci line graph. The lfitci will produce a simple bivariate linear regression between prestige and hours. It will also plot the confidence interval around the regression line. twoway (lfitci prestg80 hrs1), scheme(s2mono) title("Regress working hours onto prestige") caption("Source: General Social Survey of 2026") Regress working hours onto occupational prestige 1.3 Interpretations We have four way to interpret a simple linear regression depending on the transformation of the dependent or independent variable. Question: what does \(\beta_0\) represent? 1.3.2 Linear-Log Model \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 ln(x_i) + \varepsilon_i \] Let’s run a linear-log model where the dependent variable is not log transformed but the independent variable is log transformed. We interpret \(\beta_1\) as a \(1\%\) increase in \(x\) is associated with a \(\frac{\beta_1}{100}\) increase in \(y\) regress prestg80 lnhrs1 Source | SS df MS Number of obs = 2,715 -------------+---------------------------------- F(1, 2713) = 48.89 Model | 9594.06348 1 9594.06348 Prob > F = 0.0000 Residual | 532432.196 2,713 196.252192 R-squared = 0.0177 -------------+---------------------------------- Adj R-squared = 0.0173 Total | 542026.259 2,714 199.714908 Root MSE = 14.009 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ prestg80 | Coefficient Std. err. t P>|t| [95% conf. interval] -------------+---------------------------------------------------------------- lnhrs1 | 4.115376 .5885935 6.99 0.000 2.961239 5.269513 _cons | 29.58522 2.170863 13.63 0.000 25.3285 33.84193 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ We reject the null hypothesis that \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) at the 0.1% level and we interpret this as a \(1\%\) increase in hours is associated with a \(\frac{4.12}{100}=0.0412\) increase in prestige. 1.3.3 Log-Linear Model \[ ln(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i \] Let’s run a log-linear model, where the dependent variable is log transformed but the independent variable is not log transformed.
